title: [Docs] TlsBackend.Auto and TLS capability comments say BouncyCastle has no chain validation and SslStream uses reflection
body:
## Summary
The public XML doc of TlsBackend.Auto and comments in TlsPlatformCapabilities state that BouncyCastle does not perform full chain validation, while TlsProviderSelector and TurboTlsAuthentication show that it validates chains through ServerCertificateVerifier. Comments in the SslStream provider still describe a reflection-based ALPN path. Customers reading IntelliSense and agents following platform.md get a wrong picture of the security posture and the reason Auto stays on SslStream.

## Location
- `Runtime/Core/TlsBackend.cs:14`

## Problem
TlsBackend.Auto's public XML doc says 'BouncyCastle does not yet perform full chain validation, so Auto always uses SslStream' (Runtime/Core/TlsBackend.cs:11-16); TlsProviderSelector.GetAutoProvider's doc says the opposite ('BouncyCastle validates chains through ServerCertificateVerifier with the OS verifier', TlsProviderSelector.cs:210-215) and that is what the code does (TurboTlsAuthentication.cs:53-81). The same stale rationale is in TlsPlatformCapabilities.cs:19-20 and :167-169. BouncyCastleTlsProvider's summary says 'Guaranteed to work on all platforms, including IL2CPP/AOT builds' (BouncyCastleTlsProvider.cs:17-20) while the provider rejects every certificate on Linux (ServerCertificateVerifier.cs:239-241) and #447 is open for IL2CPP iOS stalls. Reflection-era leftovers contradict the 'without reflection (#303)' class doc (SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:16-19): IsAlpnSetupFailure still filters TargetInvocationException and MemberAccessException (:258-259), which a direct call cannot raise; TlsProviderSelector comments refer to 'ALPN reflection paths' and 'MethodInfo.Invoke' (:179-180, :195-198). The agent guide Development~/docs/agents/platform.md:11-15 still says BouncyCastle uses X509Chain on desktop and fails closed on iOS/Android 'until the native verifiers land', and open issues #303 and #35 describe reflection code that no longer exists.

**Failure scenario.** A customer reading IntelliSense for TlsBackend concludes the BouncyCastle backend does not validate certificate chains and rejects the only HTTP/2 path on Unity, or an agent following platform.md re-implements an X509Chain desktop path. A reviewer trusting IsAlpnSetupFailure's list assumes reflection is still in play.

## Suggested fix
Rewrite the TlsBackend.Auto and TlsPlatformCapabilities text to the real reason Auto stays on SslStream (explicit opt-in, verifiers not device-validated), fix the BouncyCastleTlsProvider summary, remove the dead filter arms and reflection comments, update platform.md and close or retitle #303/#35.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] TlsBackend.Auto XML doc, TlsPlatformCapabilities comments and the BouncyCastleTlsProvider summary state the real reason Auto stays on SslStream and no longer claim missing chain validation
- [ ] Dead filter arms and stale reflection comments in the TLS provider code are removed
- [ ] platform.md is updated to match, and #303 and #35 are retitled or closed if the text no longer applies

title: [TLS] BouncyCastleTlsProvider disposes the inner stream inline in token callbacks, so a blocking Dispose runs on the cancelling thread
body:
## Summary
ct.Register and deadline.Token.Register call innerStream.Dispose() synchronously on whichever thread invokes Cancel(). For SAEA and poll/select streams Dispose shuts the socket down and spin-waits for in-flight completions for up to a bound, so a main-thread cancel can block it. The effect is a UI hitch when a request or WebSocket connect is cancelled during a handshake.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/BouncyCastle/BouncyCastleTlsProvider.cs:105`

## Problem
ct.Register(DisposeStream, innerStream) and deadline.Token.Register(DisposeStream, innerStream) (BouncyCastleTlsProvider.cs:105-106, 162-165) run innerStream.Dispose() synchronously on the thread that calls Cancel(). SaeaStream.Dispose -> SaeaSocketChannel.Dispose shuts the socket down and spin-waits up to DisposeDrainTimeoutMs twice for in-flight completions (SaeaSocketChannel.cs:324-341, 355-367; #168 for completions Mono may never post); PollSelect joins its poll thread with the same bound. The registrations are redundant for correctness: the catch at lines 125-135 disposes the stream anyway once the abandon race fires, on a pool thread. The finally at lines 140-141 additionally blocks the WrapAsync continuation until a running callback returns. The SslStream provider does not do this (its dispose runs in the catch after a RunContinuationsAsynchronously signal).

**Failure scenario.** A MonoBehaviour cancels a request from the main thread (OnDestroy, a cancel button) while a BouncyCastle handshake over SocketIoMode.Saea has a receive pending whose abort completion is late or never posted on IL2CPP: the main thread spins in WaitForInFlightOperations for up to about 1 s inside CancellationTokenSource.Cancel(). Needs a device to observe the late-completion case; the inline call is traced.

## Suggested fix
Drop the two registrations and rely on the abandon race plus the dispose in the catch (pool thread), or make the callback only signal and dispose asynchronously.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Cancelling a token during a BouncyCastle handshake returns from CancellationTokenSource.Cancel() without running the socket-stream Dispose on the cancelling thread
- [ ] The abandon race and the pool-thread dispose in the catch path still release the stream exactly once on success, failure, cancellation and deadline
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ with a blocking-Dispose inner stream that fails before the fix
- [ ] Main-thread cancel latency on a late-completion socket validated on a device and recorded

title: [TLS] Non-certificate TLS handshake failures surface as UHttpErrorType.CertificateError with the real reason only in an inner exception
body:
## Summary
BouncyCastleTlsProvider maps 26 fatal alerts, and SslStreamTlsProvider maps a TLS 1.0/1.1 peer, to AuthenticationException, and RawSocketTransport turns every AuthenticationException into CertificateError. Alerts such as handshake_failure, protocol_version and no_application_protocol are negotiation failures, not certificate verdicts. Applications and security telemetry report a certificate problem and the actionable detail is lost.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/BouncyCastle/BouncyCastleTlsProvider.cs:226`

## Problem
The provider/transport contract is 'AuthenticationException = final verdict, IOException = transient'. BouncyCastleTlsProvider.IsNonTransientAlert (:241-275) maps 26 alerts to AuthenticationException, including handshake_failure, protocol_version, insufficient_security, unexpected_message, decode_error, illegal_parameter, missing_extension and no_application_protocol; SslStreamTlsProvider.EnsureMinimumTlsVersion throws AuthenticationException for a TLS 1.0/1.1 peer (SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:418-426) and SslStream itself throws it for any handshake failure. RawSocketTransport maps every AuthenticationException to CertificateError (RawSocketTransport.cs:819-821), documented in Core as 'SSL/TLS certificate validation failure' (UHttpError.cs:20-21). The message is the generic alert text: MapFatalAlert builds 'TLS handshake failed: fatal alert X sent to the server' (:226-233) and the specific reason raised by TurboTlsAuthentication (host mismatch with the SAN list, 'TlsBackend.BouncyCastle is unsupported on Linux...', verifier detail) lives only in the TlsFatalAlert two levels down; Tools~/tls-interop/Program.cs:270 has to search ex.ToString() for it. Related misclassifications on the same boundary: a provider PlatformNotSupportedException (TlsProviderSelector.cs:224, SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:294/:410) hits 'case NotSupportedException' and becomes a retryable NetworkError 'Unsupported HTTP response: ...' (RawSocketTransport.cs:814-818); the missing-define InvalidOperationException becomes Unknown (:826-827). Open issue #451 tracks only the test side of this (negative rows pass on a broken TLS stack); it does not propose changing the production classification.

**Failure scenario.** A server that only offers CBC suites or TLS 1.1 answers the BouncyCastle ClientHello with handshake_failure/protocol_version: the app receives UHttpErrorType.CertificateError with message 'fatal alert handshake_failure(40) received from the server' and reports a certificate problem to the user or to security telemetry. On Linux with BouncyCastle selected, UHttpError.Message is 'fatal alert certificate_unknown(46) sent to the server'; the actionable 'unsupported on Linux, use Auto' text is only in InnerException.InnerException.Message.

## Suggested fix
Have the providers throw one TurboHTTP TLS exception type that carries a category (certificate, negotiation, platform capability, configuration) and the detail text, and map that explicitly in RawSocketTransport instead of switching on BCL types; include the TlsFatalAlert detail in the outer message. If the public enum cannot grow before 1.0, at least put the reason in UHttpError.Message.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Providers throw one TurboHTTP TLS exception type carrying a category (certificate, negotiation, platform capability, configuration) and detail text
- [ ] RawSocketTransport maps the categories explicitly; only certificate and verifier rejections yield CertificateError, others stay non-retryable with a distinct error or stable detail
- [ ] UHttpError.Message includes the TlsFatalAlert description and the Linux unsupported-platform hint
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ for handshake_failure and protocol_version mapping that fails before the fix

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `tls-design-04` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/tls.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: code-smell.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. IsNonTransientAlert maps handshake_failure, protocol_version, insufficient_security, unexpected_message, decode_error, illegal_parameter, missing_extension, no_application_protocol and others to AuthenticationException (BouncyCastleTlsProvider.cs:226-275); SslStreamTlsProvider.EnsureMinimumTlsVersion throws it for TLS < 1.2 (SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:418-426); MapDispatchAttemptFailure turns every AuthenticationException into CertificateError with only the outer message (RawSocketTransport.cs:819-821), documented as 'SSL/TLS certificate validation failure' (UHttpError.cs:20-21). The detail raised in TurboTlsAuthentication (host mismatch, Linux-unsupported text) is only in the nested TlsFatalAlert; the interop harness has to search ex.ToString() (Tools~/tls-interop/Program.cs:270). Also confirmed: PlatformNotSupportedException from the selector/provider (TlsProviderSelector.cs:224, SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:294, :409) matches 'case NotSupportedException' first and becomes NetworkError 'Unsupported HTTP response: ...' (RawSocketTransport.cs:814-818), which IsRetryable() treats as retryable (UHttpError.cs:72-74); the missing-define InvalidOperationException (TlsProviderSelector.cs:90) falls to Unknown (:826-827). #451 states the same root cause but tracks only the test side (negative rows passing on a broken TLS stack); the production classification and message are not tracked, so the issue understates it.

Related: #451, [[R11-tls-protocol-08]].

title: [TLS] Negotiation failures (handshake_failure, protocol_version, unrecognized_name) are reported as CertificateError
body:
## Summary
IsNonTransientAlert maps non-certificate alerts to AuthenticationException, and RawSocketTransport maps every AuthenticationException to UHttpErrorType.CertificateError. A server with no common cipher suite, a TLS 1.0/1.1-only server or an SNI rejection is therefore shown as a certificate problem. RFC 8446 section 6.2 defines these as negotiation alerts, distinct from certificate alerts.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/BouncyCastle/BouncyCastleTlsProvider.cs:241`

## Problem
IsNonTransientAlert (lines 241-275) maps handshake_failure, protocol_version, illegal_parameter, decode_error, insufficient_security, unrecognized_name, no_application_protocol and others to AuthenticationException (MapFatalAlert, lines 226-233). SslStreamTlsProvider.EnsureMinimumTlsVersion throws AuthenticationException for a sub-1.2 version (SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:418-426). RawSocketTransport maps every AuthenticationException to UHttpErrorType.CertificateError (RawSocketTransport.cs:819-821), documented as 'SSL/TLS certificate validation failure' (Runtime/Core/UHttpError.cs:20). Tests assert it: Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/BouncyCastleFatalAlertTests.cs:93-94.

**Failure scenario.** A server with no cipher suite in common with the ECDHE+AEAD list, or one that only speaks TLS 1.0/1.1, or rejects the SNI name: the application gets CertificateError and shows or logs a certificate problem for what is a protocol negotiation failure. #451 tracks the testing side of the same conflation.

## Spec reference
RFC 8446 section 6.2

## Suggested fix
Keep these non-retryable but distinguish them (a dedicated error type, or a stable detail on UHttpError) so only certificate/identity alerts and verifier rejections surface as CertificateError.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Non-certificate alerts and the TLS below 1.2 rejection stay non-retryable but are distinguishable from certificate and identity failures
- [ ] Only certificate and identity alerts and verifier rejections surface as UHttpErrorType.CertificateError
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ covering a handshake_failure alert that fails before the fix

title: [TLS] BouncyCastleTlsStream 16 KiB plaintext chunk makes each full record two SAEA sends (send buffer is 16 KiB)
body:
## Summary
PlaintextChunkSize is 16 KiB, so a full record is 16405-16413 bytes, but SaeaSocketChannel sends at most its 16 KiB pinned buffer per operation. Every full record therefore needs one 16384-byte send and one tail send of about 25 bytes. Uploads and HTTP/2 DATA over BouncyCastle with SocketIoMode.Saea double the send operations and selector wake-ups.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/BouncyCastle/BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:40`

## Problem
PlaintextChunkSize is 16 * 1024 (BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:40); EncryptChunk feeds exactly that much to WriteApplicationData (lines 370, 388), producing a record of 16405-16413 bytes that DrainOutputHoldingGateAsync hands to the inner stream in one WriteAsync (line 497). SaeaSocketChannel copies into a pinned 16 * 1024 buffer and sends at most that per operation (Runtime/Transport/Tcp/SaeaSocketChannel.cs:43, 231), so the record becomes one 16384-byte send and one 21-29 byte send. With NoDelay the tail can leave as its own segment. PollSelect sends from the caller's array and NetworkStream sends in one call, so only SAEA is affected.

**Failure scenario.** Upload or HTTP/2 DATA over BouncyCastle with SocketIoMode.Saea (the mode sold as the low-overhead path): the number of SAEA send operations, selector wake-ups and completion callbacks per megabyte doubles (128 instead of 64), each tail send carrying about 25 bytes.

## Suggested fix
Size the plaintext chunk so a record fits the inner send unit (for example 16 KiB minus 64 bytes), or coalesce several records per inner write; alternatively make the SAEA send buffer at least one maximum record.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A full TLS record is written to the inner stream in one socket send operation (chunk size reduced or SAEA send buffer enlarged)
- [ ] Send operations per MiB of upload over BouncyCastle SAEA drop from 128 to 64 or fewer, measured
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ counting inner send operations per full record, failing before the fix

title: [TLS] BouncyCastleTlsStream allocates about 37 KiB of unpooled buffers per connection plus a new SecureRandom and BcTlsCrypto per handshake
body:
## Summary
Each BouncyCastleTlsStream allocates two 18437-byte arrays for its lifetime and two optional 16 KiB scratch arrays, and each handshake creates a new SecureRandom that seeds its own digest generator. Transport buffers elsewhere are pooled. Connection churn on mobile produces GC spikes.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/BouncyCastle/BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:59`

## Problem
_readBuffer and _writeBuffer are new byte[CiphertextBufferSize] (18437 bytes each, BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:44, 59, 63) for the life of every connection, with two more lazily allocated 16 KiB scratch arrays for non-array Memory (lines 381, 410). BouncyCastleTlsProvider.HandshakeAsync creates new BcTlsCrypto(new SecureRandom()) per handshake (BouncyCastleTlsProvider.cs:179), each SecureRandom auto-seeding its own digest generator. Nothing is rented from ByteArrayPool (Core.Internal is not visible to this assembly: Runtime/Core/AssemblyInfo.cs has no InternalsVisibleTo for TurboHTTP.Transport.BouncyCastle), although the transport rule is pooled network buffers. Returning them is safe on a normal Dispose; only the abandoned-handshake path (#344) must keep them.

**Failure scenario.** Connection churn (servers that close after each response, retries on a flaky mobile network, WebSocket reconnect loops): each new TLS connection adds about 37 KiB of garbage plus the per-handshake crypto objects, which shows up as GC spikes on mobile where the rest of the transport pools its buffers.

## Suggested fix
Rent the two ciphertext buffers (through a Transport-internal forwarder to ByteArrayPool) and return them in Dispose when no read or write is in flight, abandoning them otherwise; share one SecureRandom (it is thread-safe) across handshakes.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Ciphertext buffers are rented from the pool and returned exactly once in Dispose, or abandoned when an I/O is in flight
- [ ] One thread-safe SecureRandom is shared across handshakes
- [ ] Managed allocation per new TLS connection drops by at least 36 KiB, measured and recorded
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ for buffer return on success, failure and dispose during I/O

title: [TLS] BouncyCastleTlsStream.Dispose sends close_notify with a blocking synchronous write, sync-over-async on SAEA and poll/select streams
body:
## Summary
Dispose calls the inner stream's synchronous Write, which on SaeaStream and PollSelectStream is WriteAsync(...).GetAwaiter().GetResult(), and the inner stream is disposed only afterwards. When pool workers are saturated, each Dispose blocks a worker waiting for a send completion that needs a free worker, and from the main thread UHttpClient.Dispose blocks per connection. This violates the no sync-over-async rule.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/BouncyCastle/BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:271`

## Problem
Dispose (BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:258-294) calls _protocol.Close(), then if _writeGate.Wait(0) succeeds runs DrainOutputHoldingGate (line 501-508), which calls _inner.Write(_writeBuffer, 0, count) synchronously; _inner.Dispose() is only reached in the finally after that write returns. SaeaStream.Write is WriteAsync(...).GetAwaiter().GetResult() (Runtime/Transport/Tcp/SaeaStream.cs:91-92) and PollSelectStream.Write is the same (PollSelectStream.cs:86-87). On Mono/IL2CPP Socket.SendAsync(SocketAsyncEventArgs) completes through the I/O selector and a pool worker (the repo's own analysis on #206 and the test header of Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/BouncyCastleHandshakeThreadPoolTests.cs:15-17 state that a synchronous Read/Write over SaeaStream needs a second pool thread). In NetworkStream mode it is a blocking Socket.Send with no SendTimeout (no SendTimeout is set anywhere under Runtime/). Every BouncyCastle connection close goes through this: PooledConnection.Dispose -> Stream.Dispose (TcpConnectionPool.cs:139-142), from pool scavenging and async continuations (pool workers) and from UHttpClient.Dispose (usually the Unity main thread). The thread-pool test avoids the path on purpose (BouncyCastleHandshakeThreadPoolTests.cs:184-185: 'Dispose's best-effort close_notify is synchronous by contract ... the stream is released by the socket cleanup instead'), and BouncyCastleSocketModeTests also disposes the socket, not the TLS stream, so no test covers Dispose over SAEA.

**Failure scenario.** SocketIoMode.Saea + TlsBackend.BouncyCastle (the HTTP/2 configuration): N connections are closed from pool workers while the pool is saturated (burst of failures, scavenger, shutdown). Each Dispose blocks its worker in GetResult() waiting for a send completion that itself needs a free worker; with all workers inside Dispose nothing completes until Mono injects threads (about one per 500 ms), or never with a capped pool. From the main thread, UHttpClient.Dispose blocks one selector round trip per idle connection. In any mode, if the kernel send buffer is full and no writer holds the gate, the write never returns and _inner.Dispose() is never reached (no token, no timeout).

## Suggested fix
Do not block in Dispose: skip close_notify unless it can be handed off without waiting (e.g. start the async drain with an owner that disposes the inner stream when it ends or after a short bound), and add a DisposeAsync that awaits the async drain for callers that can. Add a test that disposes the TLS stream over SaeaStream with the pool clamped.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] BouncyCastleTlsStream.Dispose never blocks on an inner stream write; close_notify is skipped or handed off with an owner that disposes the inner stream when it ends or after a short bound
- [ ] A DisposeAsync awaits the asynchronous drain for callers that can
- [ ] Inner stream is disposed exactly once on every path
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ disposing the TLS stream over SaeaStream with the pool clamped, failing before the fix

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `tls-runtime-01` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/tls.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: concurrency.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. Dispose (BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:258-294) calls _protocol.Close(), then on _writeGate.Wait(0) runs DrainOutputHoldingGate (:501-508) -> _inner.Write synchronously; _inner.Dispose() is only in the finally after the write returns. SaeaStream.Write is WriteAsync(...).GetAwaiter().GetResult() (SaeaStream.cs:91-92), PollSelectStream.Write likewise (PollSelectStream.cs:86-87): sync-over-async, which CLAUDE.md section 4 bans. Every pooled BouncyCastle connection closes through it (PooledConnection.Dispose -> Stream.Dispose, TcpConnectionPool.cs:139-143). No SendTimeout exists under Runtime/ (rg), so in NetworkStream mode the write is an unbounded blocking send when the kernel buffer is full and no writer holds the gate. The repo acknowledges and sidesteps it in the test (BouncyCastleHandshakeThreadPoolTests.cs:15-17 and :184-185 'Dispose's best-effort close_notify is synchronous by contract ... released by the socket cleanup instead'), so nothing covers Dispose over SAEA. Limits on impact: SocketIoMode.Saea is opt-in (default NetworkStream, ConnectionPoolOptions.cs:62) and BouncyCastle is opt-in; in the default mode a 31-byte send normally returns at once; under SAEA the stall lasts until the pool injects a thread unless the pool is capped. Not tracked (#447 is the handshake path, #168 is SaeaSocketChannel.Dispose).

Also reported as `tls-design-13` (merged into this issue).

Related: #168, #447, [[R11-tls-runtime-09]].

title: [TLS] BouncyCastleTlsStream uses Task-returning byte[] overloads that allocate per read and write on the inner stream
body:
## Summary
The adapter calls the byte[] ReadAsync and WriteAsync overloads of the inner stream, which SaeaStream implements with AsTask(), and returns Task<int> for reads whose plaintext is already decrypted. Each frame read allocates a Task<int> and each ciphertext operation a wrapper Task. This adds garbage on the SAEA path meant to be allocation-free.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/BouncyCastle/BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:319`

## Problem
Inbound: ReadCoreAsync and HandshakeAsync call _inner.ReadAsync(_readBuffer, 0, len, ct) (BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:123, 319) and DrainOutputHoldingGateAsync calls _inner.WriteAsync(byte[], int, int, CancellationToken) (line 497). SaeaStream implements those overloads as _channel.ReceiveAsync(...).AsTask() / SendAsync(...).AsTask() (SaeaStream.cs:52-57, 94-99), adding a Task wrapper per operation on top of the channel's own state machine, while its Memory overloads return the ValueTask directly (SaeaStream.cs:59-72, 101-106). Outbound to callers: ReadAsync(byte[], ...) returns ReadCoreAsync(...).AsTask() (lines 157-161), so even a synchronously completed read of buffered plaintext allocates a Task<int>; there is no cached last-result task. Http2FrameCodec reads every frame header and payload through that overload (Http2FrameCodec.cs:260), as do the HTTP/1.1 parser fill reads (Http11ResponseParser.cs:1379, 1415).

**Failure scenario.** HTTP/2 download over BouncyCastle: each frame header read and each payload read allocates a Task<int> (about 72 bytes) although the plaintext is already in the engine, plus one wrapper Task per ciphertext read and per record write on SAEA: several hundred bytes of garbage per frame on the path the SAEA mode exists to keep allocation-free (related measurements for other paths: #434, #416).

## Suggested fix
Call the Memory-based ValueTask overloads of the inner stream, and cache the last synchronously completed Task<int> in ReadAsync(byte[], ...) (as BufferedStream/MemoryStream do) or move the frame codec to the Memory overload.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Inner reads and writes use the Memory-based ValueTask overloads
- [ ] Synchronously completed Task<int> results are cached for the byte[] ReadAsync overload, or the caller uses the Memory overload
- [ ] Managed allocations per HTTP/2 frame read over BouncyCastle SAEA reduced to zero for already-decrypted data, measured
- [ ] Deterministic allocation test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ that fails before the fix

title: [TLS] Failed write of a reply record fails a BouncyCastle read that already holds decrypted data or a clean close_notify
body:
## Summary
ReadCoreAsync awaits FlushPendingOutputAsync after ProcessCiphertext, outside any try, so an inner write failure propagates out of the read before queued plaintext or the peer's close_notify is delivered. A server that sends an early response (for example 413 with Connection: close) and closes with unread request bytes can reset the connection, making the client lose a response it already received. RFC 8446 section 6.1 treats close_notify as a clean end of data.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/BouncyCastle/BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:332`

## Problem
ReadCoreAsync: after ProcessCiphertext(read) succeeds, `await FlushPendingOutputAsync()` (line 332; sync twin line 195) runs outside any try, so an inner WriteAsync failure propagates out of the read. ProcessCiphertext may have just queued plaintext and processed the peer's close_notify, for which the engine queues its own close_notify (Lib/tls/TlsProtocol.cs HandleClose -> RaiseAlertWarning(close_notify)). The loop only returns plaintext on the next iteration (TryReadPlaintext, line 316), which is never reached. The handshake path and Dispose treat the same flush as best effort (lines 143-150, 283-286).

**Failure scenario.** Server answers early (for example 413 with Connection: close) while the client is still uploading, sends the response and close_notify, then closes with unread request bytes, so the kernel resets the connection. The client's inner read still returns the response records and the close_notify; the engine queues the close_notify reply; the body writer has already failed and released the gate, so the reader takes it and its write fails with EPIPE/ECONNRESET. The read throws IOException: response bytes that arrived in the same read are dropped and a close-delimited body that ended with a proper close_notify is reported as a network error. Confirm with a loopback server that sends data + close_notify and resets before the client flushes.

## Spec reference
RFC 8446 section 6.1

## Suggested fix
After ProcessCiphertext succeeded, make the read-path flush best effort when plaintext is queued or the engine is closed (catch the write failure, deliver the plaintext/EOF, let the write path report the dead socket).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] After ProcessCiphertext succeeds, a failed reply flush is best effort when plaintext is queued or the engine is closed, and the plaintext or EOF is delivered

title: [TLS] BouncyCastleTlsStream read path awaits a non-cancellable output flush before returning already decrypted plaintext
body:
## Summary
After ProcessCiphertext the read awaits FlushPendingOutputAsync, which writes with CancellationToken.None, before it returns plaintext. If the engine queued output (KeyUpdate, no_renegotiation) and the local send buffer is full, the read blocks holding decrypted data and ignores its token. The documented rule that a stalled write cannot block a read is not met on this path.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/BouncyCastle/BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:332`

## Problem
After ProcessCiphertext, ReadCoreAsync awaits FlushPendingOutputAsync (BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:332) before looping back to TryReadPlaintext (line 316). When no writer holds the gate, FlushPendingOutputAsync takes it and awaits DrainOutputHoldingGateAsync, which writes with CancellationToken.None (lines 492-498, 515-527). The class remark (lines 32-33: the read path 'never takes _writeGate while waiting, so a stalled write can never block a read') and the backlog bound (lines 464-478) only cover the case where another writer already holds the gate; when the gate is free the reader itself becomes the stalled writer and EnforceOutputBacklogLimit is never reached.

**Failure scenario.** Peer sends a record that makes the engine queue output (TLS 1.3 KeyUpdate with update_requested, a TLS 1.2 hello_request answered with no_renegotiation) together with application data, while the local send buffer is full and the peer is not reading (both directions saturated, or a hostile peer repeating such records with a zero window): the reader blocks in the socket write holding decrypted application data it never returns, the caller's read token is ignored, and only disposing the stream ends it.

## Suggested fix
Return available plaintext before flushing, and make the reader's flush opportunistic (start the drain without awaiting it, owned by the gate) so the backlog bound applies uniformly.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Available plaintext is returned before the reply flush
- [ ] The reader's flush is started without awaiting it, owned by the write gate, so the backlog bound applies uniformly
- [ ] A cancelled read token ends the read while a write is stalled
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ with a stalled inner write that fails before the fix

title: [TLS] BouncyCastleTlsStream sends every write call as its own TLS record and socket send, so each HTTP/2 frame costs two records
body:
## Summary
WriteCoreAsync encrypts and sends per call and FlushAsync does not coalesce. Http2FrameCodec writes the 9-byte header and the payload as separate calls, so each frame becomes two records, two AEAD operations and two NoDelay sends. On SAEA each send is a selector and pool-worker round trip.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/BouncyCastle/BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:351`

## Problem
WriteCoreAsync encrypts and drains per call (BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:351-355: EncryptChunk then DrainOutputHoldingGateAsync -> _inner.WriteAsync at line 497); FlushAsync only forwards to the inner stream (lines 241-246), so nothing is ever coalesced. Http2FrameCodec writes the 9-byte frame header and the payload as separate WriteAsync calls and flushes afterwards (Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2FrameCodec.cs:221-235). Sockets are created with NoDelay = true (Runtime/Transport/Connection/HappyEyeballsConnector.cs:491).

**Failure scenario.** HTTP/2 over BouncyCastle: a HEADERS frame of 60 bytes goes out as a 9-byte record (31-38 bytes on the wire) and a second record, i.e. two socket sends and normally two packets; a 1 MiB upload in 16 KiB DATA frames produces about 128 extra tiny records and sends. On Mono/IL2CPP SAEA each send is a full selector plus pool-worker round trip.

## Suggested fix
Coalesce at one side of the boundary: have the HTTP/2 codec write header and payload in one call, or let the TLS stream keep records in the engine's output queue until FlushAsync or a size threshold (callers that never flush must then be audited).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A frame header and payload leave in one TLS record and one socket send, via a single codec write or record coalescing until FlushAsync
- [ ] Record count per HTTP/2 frame over BouncyCastle is one, measured
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ counting records per frame that fails before the fix

title: [TLS] BouncyCastleTlsStream read pending during local Dispose can return 0 as a clean end of stream
body:
## Summary
When BouncyCastleTlsStream is disposed while a read is pending, the inner socket shutdown ends the receive with 0 bytes. The engine is closed but not failed, so ReadCoreAsync returns 0 instead of throwing. A caller that treats 0 as end of data, such as a close-delimited HTTP/1.1 body reader, would see a complete message. Current transport callers re-check their token, so this is a contract hazard rather than an observed truncation.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/BouncyCastle/BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:418`

## Problem
Dispose sets _disposed, calls _protocol.Close() (engine closed, not failed) and disposes the inner stream (lines 258-290). HoldingNetworkStream disposal shuts the socket down (Runtime/Transport/Tcp/SocketHandleHold.cs:235), which ends a pending receive with 0 bytes. ReadCoreAsync does not re-check _disposed after the await (lines 319-333): ProcessCiphertext(0) calls CloseInput, which returns silently when the engine is already closed (Lib/tls/TlsProtocol.cs:1235-1236), and TryReadPlaintext then returns 0 because IsClosed && !IsFailed (lines 418-425). RawSocketTransport.RegisterDisposeOnCancel (RawSocketTransport.cs:319-324) does Shutdown then Dispose, so the result is IOException or 0 depending on which thread wins.

**Failure scenario.** A close-delimited HTTP/1.1 body (or any loop that treats 0 as end of data) is being read; another thread disposes the connection (Abort, client dispose, cancel callback). The reader gets 0 = complete message instead of ObjectDisposedException/IOException. Current transport callers re-check their token after the read, so this is a contract hazard rather than an observed truncation.

## Spec reference
RFC 8446 section 6.1

## Suggested fix
After the inner read returns, and in TryReadPlaintext when the engine is closed, throw ObjectDisposedException if _disposed is set; return 0 only for a close initiated by the peer's close_notify.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A read pending when the stream is disposed locally throws ObjectDisposedException or IOException and never returns 0
- [ ] 0 is returned only after a close_notify from the peer
- [ ] Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ contains a deterministic NUnit test that disposes the stream during a pending read and fails before the fix

title: [TLS] TurboTlsAuthentication copies server-controlled dNSName values unsanitised into the handshake exception text
body:
## Summary
ValidateHostname joins every dNSName from the server certificate into the TlsFatalAlert message. The names can contain CR, LF and other control characters and can total up to about 30 KiB. The message is kept in the exception chain that logs and crash reports print, so a hostile server can forge log lines and inflate log volume.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/BouncyCastle/TurboTlsAuthentication.cs:145`

## Problem
ValidateHostname builds the TlsFatalAlert message from `string.Join(", ", dnsNames)` (lines 145-147). The names come from IA5String values (line 124) and may contain CR, LF and other control characters; their total size is bounded only by the 32 KiB handshake-message cap (Lib/tls/AbstractTlsPeer.cs:59). The alert is kept as the inner exception of the AuthenticationException (BouncyCastleTlsProvider.cs:231) and of the UHttpError (RawSocketTransport.cs:820-821).

**Failure scenario.** A hostile or intercepting server presents a certificate with a dNSName such as "x\n[TurboHTTP] request ok ..." repeated up to ~30 KiB. Any log, monitor entry or crash report that prints the exception chain records forged lines and tens of kilobytes of attacker text per failed connection.

## Suggested fix
Report the count of dNSName entries (as already done for iPAddress entries), or include at most a few names after stripping non-printable characters and capping the length.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The hostname-mismatch exception reports the count of dNSName entries, or at most a few names with non-printable characters stripped and the length capped
- [ ] No server-controlled string longer than a fixed cap (stated in the code) appears in the exception message
- [ ] Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ contains a deterministic NUnit test using a certificate with CR/LF and oversized dNSName values that fails before the fix

title: [TLS] TurboTlsClient accepts a server-selected ALPN protocol that the client did not offer
body:
## Summary
NotifyHandshakeComplete copies the server's ALPN selection into NegotiatedAlpn without checking that it was in the offered list. The vendored engine rejects only unsolicited extensions. A server or middlebox can select an unoffered name such as spdy/3.1, or h2 when only http/1.1 was offered, and the handshake succeeds while the two ends speak different protocols.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/BouncyCastle/TurboTlsClient.cs:165`

## Problem
NotifyHandshakeComplete copies securityParams.ApplicationProtocol into NegotiatedAlpn (lines 165-169). The vendored engine stores whatever single name the server sent (Lib/tls/TlsClientProtocol.cs:1331 and 1467, GetAlpnExtensionServer) and AbstractTlsClient.ProcessServerExtensions (Lib/tls/AbstractTlsClient.cs:455-495) has no membership check; only an unsolicited extension is rejected. Callers compensate in one place only: RawSocketTransport.IsHttp2Tunnel (RawSocketTransport.cs:1419-1420) ignores an unoffered h2 in a CONNECT tunnel.

**Failure scenario.** Client offers [h2, http/1.1]; a server (or an on-path device terminating TLS) selects 'spdy/3.1' or any other name. The handshake succeeds, TlsResult.NegotiatedAlpn is that name, and the pool routes the connection as HTTP/1.1 (RawSocketTransport.cs:622 tests only for "h2"), so both ends speak different protocols on an authenticated connection instead of the handshake failing. With Http11Only offered and 'h2' returned, the client speaks HTTP/1.1 to a peer that announced h2.

## Spec reference
RFC 7301 section 3.1/3.2

## Suggested fix
In TurboTlsClient, compare the selected protocol with _alpnProtocols during the handshake (NotifySelectedProtocol / before NotifyHandshakeComplete) and raise TlsFatalAlert(illegal_parameter) when it was not offered.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] TurboTlsClient raises TlsFatalAlert(illegal_parameter) when the selected ALPN name is not in the offered list
- [ ] Handshakes where the selection is a member of the offered list are unchanged
- [ ] Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ contains a deterministic NUnit test with a server that selects an unoffered protocol and fails before the fix

title: [Transport] RawSocketTransport and TcpConnectionPool each store the TLS backend, so tunnelled and direct HTTPS can use different providers
body:
## Summary
The public RawSocketTransport constructor accepts a pool and an independent tlsBackend, and each keeps its own copy. Direct HTTPS handshakes use the pool's backend, while handshakes inside a CONNECT tunnel use the transport's backend and bypass the pool's provider-resolver seam. A hand-built combination silently uses BouncyCastle for direct traffic and SslStream for proxied traffic, or the reverse, with no error or log.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/RawSocketTransport.cs:1455`

## Problem
RawSocketTransport's public constructor takes an optional pool and an independent tlsBackend (RawSocketTransport.cs:42, :58-75): when a pool is passed, the pool keeps the backend it was built with (TcpConnectionPool.cs:281, :323) and the transport stores its own copy (_tlsBackend, :75). Direct HTTPS handshakes resolve the provider from the pool's value (TcpConnectionPool.cs:681-683), but the handshake inside a CONNECT tunnel resolves it from the transport's value (RawSocketTransport.cs:1455 TlsProviderSelector.GetProvider(_tlsBackend)), which also bypasses the pool's provider-resolver seam. Nothing compares the two values; the pool does not expose its backend. Only the built-in factory passes the same value to both (RawSocketTransport.cs:107-121).

**Failure scenario.** new RawSocketTransport(pool: new TcpConnectionPool(tlsBackend: TlsBackend.BouncyCastle)) (tlsBackend defaults to Auto): direct https requests handshake with BouncyCastle (ALPN, h2, OS verifier bridge), requests through an HTTP proxy handshake with SslStream (no ALPN on Unity, HTTP/1.1, different certificate verifier). The reverse call, new RawSocketTransport(customPool, TlsBackend.BouncyCastle), uses SslStream for all direct traffic while the caller believes BouncyCastle is selected. No error or log in either case.

## Suggested fix
Give the backend one owner: let the pool own provider resolution (expose a WrapAsync/ResolveTlsProvider on TcpConnectionPool used by the tunnel path) or have the transport read the pool's backend and reject a mismatch in the constructor.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The TLS backend has a single owner: the pool resolves the provider for both direct and tunnelled handshakes, or the constructor rejects a mismatch
- [ ] The tunnel handshake goes through the pool's provider-resolver seam
- [ ] Tests/Runtime/Transport/ contains a deterministic NUnit test constructing the transport with a mismatched pool and backend that fails before the fix

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `tls-design-02` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/tls.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: low. Angle: architecture.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. The public constructor takes an optional pool and an independent backend and stores its own copy (RawSocketTransport.cs:42, :58-75); the public TcpConnectionPool constructor takes its own tlsBackend (TcpConnectionPool.cs:321-323, :360). Direct handshakes use the pool's value and resolver seam (TcpConnectionPool.cs:681-683); the tunnel handshake uses the transport's value and bypasses the seam (RawSocketTransport.cs:1455, :1464). Nothing compares them and the pool exposes no backend. Only the built-in factory passes the same value to both (:107-121). Downgraded: reachable only by hand-constructing transport and pool with different values; both providers validate certificates, so the effect is a silent protocol/provider difference on proxied requests (HTTP/1.1 instead of h2), not a security or correctness break.

Also reported as `net-design-04`, `net-protocol-20` (merged into this issue).

title: [TLS] ITlsProvider contract omits required validation and WebSocketConnectionOptions.TlsProvider can silently replace certificate validation
body:
## Summary
ITlsProvider is public but its documentation does not require chain and host-name validation, a TLS 1.2 floor or a handshake bound. WebSocketConnectionOptions.TlsProvider replaces the built-in provider selection for wss:// connections. A provider written for testing that accepts every certificate leaves those connections unauthenticated, with nothing in the API or docs marking this as caller responsibility.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/ITlsProvider.cs:12`

## Problem
ITlsProvider is public and its contract (lines 8-37) describes host as 'for SNI and certificate validation' but never requires chain and host-name validation, a TLS 1.2 floor or a handshake bound. RawSocketWebSocketTransport.ResolveTlsProvider (Runtime/WebSocket.Transport/RawSocketWebSocketTransport.cs:286-296) uses options.TlsProvider in place of TlsProviderSelector; the option is documented only as 'Optional TLS provider override' (Runtime/WebSocket/WebSocketConnectionOptions.cs:107-111). The HTTP transport has no such override, and no file under Documentation~ mentions custom providers.

**Failure scenario.** An application supplies a provider written for local testing (accept-all callback) through WebSocketConnectionOptions.TlsProvider; every wss:// connection made with those options is unauthenticated, and nothing in the API or docs marks this as the one place where the library's 'never accept what the platform rejects' rule is delegated to the caller.

## Suggested fix
Document on ITlsProvider and on the option that the provider is solely responsible for chain and host validation, and that the built-in ones can only be selected, not relaxed; consider making the override internal until the pinning hooks of #117 define the supported extension point.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] XML docs on ITlsProvider and WebSocketConnectionOptions.TlsProvider state that the provider alone is responsible for chain and host-name validation and for a TLS 1.2 minimum
- [ ] Either the override is made internal until the pinning hooks of #117 define the extension point, or the docs are updated and the decision is recorded
- [ ] Documentation~ describes custom providers and the validation duty; no test is needed for this documentation-only change

title: [TLS] SecTrust evaluation is implemented twice (iOS Objective-C++ and macOS C#) and CI checks only the result-code enum for drift
body:
## Summary
The iOS bridge in TurboHttpSecTrustVerifier.mm and MacSecTrustVerifier.EvaluateCore perform the same SecTrust sequence, and the errSec to result mapping exists in both with a keep-in-sync comment. check_repo.py compares only the kTurboTrust/Result constants. A code added in one file and not the other makes the same chain report different results on iOS and macOS, and CI stays green.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/MacSecTrustVerifier.cs:83`

## Problem
Plugins/iOS/TurboHttpSecTrustVerifier.mm:152-221 (Evaluate) and MacSecTrustVerifier.EvaluateCore (MacSecTrustVerifier.cs:83-154) perform the same sequence (certificate array, SecPolicyCreateSSL, SecTrustCreateWithCertificates, SetNetworkFetchAllowed(false), SetVerifyDate, SecTrustEvaluateWithError, copy chain). The error mapping exists twice with a 'keep in sync' comment: .mm:54-72 and AppleTrustVerifier.MapEvaluationError (AppleTrustVerifier.cs:107-120, hard-coded errSec values :84-89). Tools~/ci/check_repo.py:608-609 compares only the kTurboTrust*/Result* constants, not the errSec mapping or the evaluation steps. The copies have already diverged: test anchors (SecTrustSetAnchorCertificates + AnchorCertificatesOnly) exist only in C# (MacSecTrustVerifier.cs:128-139), which is why PlatformVerifierTrustsTestAnchors excludes iOS (ServerCertificateVerifier.cs:228-229); the path cap is 16 in the bridge (.mm:38) and 11 in C# (PlatformCertificateVerifier.cs:90); an empty host is a bridge error in one (.mm:234-236) and Invalid in the other (MacSecTrustVerifier.cs:58-60).

**Failure scenario.** A new errSec code is mapped in one file (as errSecCreateChainFailed was for iOS 26, #239) and forgotten in the other: the same chain is reported as UntrustedRoot on iOS and Invalid on macOS (unknown_ca vs bad_certificate alert), and CI stays green because only the enum values are compared. A hardening step added to one evaluation (for example a policy or anchor option) does not reach the other platform.

## Suggested fix
Use one implementation: validate that the C# P/Invoke path loads Security.framework on iOS IL2CPP (needs-device-validation) and retire the .mm, or build the same C source for macOS as a bundle. At minimum extend check_repo to the errSec mapping and add the anchor option to the iOS bridge so both run the same code under test.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The SecTrust evaluation has one implementation, or check_repo.py also compares the errSec mapping and the evaluation options of both files
- [ ] A hardening option added to one path is either shared or fails the check
- [ ] The check has a negative case in Tools~/ci tests that fails when the mappings differ; if the P/Invoke path replaces the .mm it is validated on an iOS IL2CPP device and recorded

title: [TLS] MacSecTrustVerifier calls SecTrustEvaluateWithError without a fallback for an OS that lacks the symbol
body:

EvaluateCore imports SecTrustEvaluateWithError (macOS 10.14, iOS 12) with no guard, while the neighbouring SecTrustCopyCertificateChain call has an EntryPointNotFoundException fallback. title: [TLS] PlatformVerifierLimits.MaxAbandoned does not bound verifier threads because in-flight calls are not counted
body:
## Summary
PlatformVerifierRunner.Run checks the abandoned counter, then starts a thread, and increments the counter only after a 10 s Join times out. Handshakes arriving in the same window all start threads regardless of MaxAbandoned. When a native verifier hangs, dozens of dedicated threads can be created and then abandoned at once, after which every BouncyCastle handshake fails fast as a certificate error.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/PlatformCertificateVerifier.cs:104`

## Problem
Run tests limits.Abandoned >= limits.MaxAbandoned (PlatformCertificateVerifier.cs:104) and then starts a thread (116-120); the counter is incremented only after a 10 s Join times out (131-133). Any number of handshakes that reach certificate verification within the same 10 s window each start a thread, whatever MaxAbandoned (4) says; the summary at lines 33-36 presents it as the bound on threads still running.

**Failure scenario.** Native verifier hangs (keystore or trustd unresponsive). 30 connections across several hosts are opened within 10 s: 30 dedicated threads (default stack reservation each, JNI-attached on Android) are created and then all abandoned; the counter jumps to 30, and from then on every BouncyCastle handshake in the process fails fast as a certificate error until those native calls return.

## Suggested fix
Count running verifications (increment before Start, decrement in Execute's finally) and refuse or queue above a fixed number, so the limit bounds threads rather than only past timeouts.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The runner counts running verifications, incrementing before the thread starts and decrementing in a finally block
- [ ] Above the fixed limit, new verifications are refused or queued, so thread count is bounded by that limit rather than by past timeouts

title: [TLS] Certificate verification blocks a thread-pool thread in Thread.Join for up to 10 s per handshake
body:
## Summary
PlatformVerifierRunner.Run creates a dedicated thread for every handshake and the caller waits in worker.Join with a 10 s default timeout. The caller is BouncyCastle's input processing, running on an I/O continuation, which is a pool worker. Several parallel HTTPS connections on a mobile device can occupy the pool until the native verifier returns. The blocking is traced; its magnitude needs a device measurement.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/PlatformCertificateVerifier.cs:131`

## Problem
PlatformVerifierRunner.Run creates a Thread per call (PlatformCertificateVerifier.cs:116-120) and waits with worker.Join(limits.Timeout) (line 131, 10 s by default, line 43-44). It is called from TurboTlsAuthentication.NotifyServerCertificate -> VerifyPath (TurboTlsAuthentication.cs:78, 203-204) -> ServerCertificateVerifier.Verify (ServerCertificateVerifier.cs:296), which BouncyCastle invokes inside _protocol.OfferInput under _protocolLock (BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:131-134). That code runs on the continuation of _inner.ReadAsync: for SaeaStream the ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore has RunContinuationsAsynchronously unset (SaeaCompletionSource.cs:37), so it runs inline on the completion callback, a pool worker on Mono/IL2CPP; for NetworkStream it is the pool thread that completed the receive. The remark at PlatformCertificateVerifier.cs:79-81 ('it is already synchronous inside BouncyCastle's input processing, so no async work is blocked on') overlooks that the blocked thread is a shared pool worker. On Android the first calls also serialize on lock(Gate) while TrustManagerFactory.init loads the key store (AndroidTrustManagerVerifier.cs:209-224), so every concurrent first handshake parks a worker for that whole time. The same worker also runs the key agreement and signature checks; there is no cap on concurrent handshakes.

**Failure scenario.** App start on a 4-8 core phone with TlsBackend.BouncyCastle: 8 parallel HTTPS connections reach the Certificate message together; 8 pool workers (the pool minimum) sit in Thread.Join until the native verifier returns (cold Android trust-manager init, or up to 10 s each if trustd/keystore is slow). During that time no other continuation or System.Threading.Timer callback runs (request timeouts, the TLS deadline itself, other requests' I/O completions) until the pool injects threads. Magnitude needs a device measurement; the blocking itself is traced.

## Suggested fix
Keep pool workers out of the wait: run the handshake's input processing on the dedicated thread (or a LongRunning task) from the point the engine is fed, or call the verifier inline where no JNI attach isolation is needed and let the existing handshake-deadline abandon bound it. At minimum bound concurrent verifications and document the cost.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Pool workers are not blocked for the duration of native verification, or the number of concurrent verifications is bounded and the cost is documented
- [ ] Pool occupancy during a slow verifier is measured on an Android device with 8 parallel handshakes and the result recorded
- [ ] Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ contains a deterministic NUnit test with a blocking verifier asserting that other continuations still run, which fails before the fix

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `tls-runtime-02` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/tls.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: low. Angle: concurrency.

Verification: Plausible: the code is as described; the outcome depends on runtime, device or peer behaviour that a static review cannot settle.

Verifier note: Code is as described: PlatformVerifierRunner.Run creates one Thread per call (PlatformCertificateVerifier.cs:116-120) and the caller waits in worker.Join(limits.Timeout) (:131, 10 s default :43-44); the caller is TurboTlsAuthentication.NotifyServerCertificate (TurboTlsAuthentication.cs:78, :203-204) inside _protocol.OfferInput under _protocolLock (BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:131-134), i.e. on the continuation of _inner.ReadAsync, a pool worker. The remark at PlatformCertificateVerifier.cs:79-81 does overlook that. But the worker it joins is a dedicated non-pool thread, so there is no pool dependency or deadlock: the pool worker is blocked exactly as long as an inline verifier call would block it (SslStream validates certificates synchronously on a pool thread too), plus one thread start (and a JNI attach on Android) per connection, not per request. The harmful case (many workers parked for hundreds of ms on cold Android TrustManagerFactory.init under lock(Gate), AndroidTrustManagerVerifier.cs:209-224, or up to 10 s on a hung verifier) depends on device verifier latency and was not measured; #428 (BC handshake benchmark on arm64) would show it. Downgraded to low.

title: [TLS] Test-only trust engine and test seams are compiled into the shipping verifier and exposed through InternalsVisibleTo
body:
## Summary
ServerCertificateVerifier.Verify branches on process-wide test anchors and an X509Chain engine with AllowUnknownCertificateAuthority, both compiled in production builds. InternalsVisibleTo grants internals to five unsigned non-shipped assembly names. Any assembly with one of those names can call AddTestTrustAnchor and make BouncyCastle connections on iOS and Android skip the OS verifier. The finding is confirmed as a design defect; the verifier judged the security framing weaker than reported.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/ServerCertificateVerifier.cs:290`

## Problem
ServerCertificateVerifier.Verify branches on a process-wide static before it reaches the platform verifier: if any test anchor is registered and the platform verifier does not take anchors itself, the chain is validated by VerifyWithX509Chain (ServerCertificateVerifier.cs:286-291) with X509VerificationFlags.AllowUnknownCertificateAuthority (:351-353) and hand-written flag filtering (:402-433). The anchors are added by internal statics AddTestTrustAnchor/RestoreTestTrustAnchors (:303-334), unconditional in production builds. Runtime/Transport/AssemblyInfo.cs:3-13 grants internals to TurboHTTP.Tests.Runtime, TurboHTTP.TlsInterop, TurboHTTP.H2Interop, TurboHTTP.Fuzz and TurboHTTP.Soak, none of which ship and none of which are strong-named, so any assembly with one of those names in a customer project compiles against AddTestTrustAnchor, RegisterPlatformVerifier (:251-256) and TlsProviderSelector.ExchangeBouncyCastleProviderForTesting (TlsProviderSelector.cs:118-123). PlatformVerifierTrustsTestAnchors is true only on Windows/macOS (:228-229), so on iOS, Android and Linux every fixture that registers an anchor is validated by X509Chain and never by SecTrust or the Android trust manager: the on-device loopback suites do not exercise the production verifier at all. RegisterPlatformVerifier is first-wins and returns false when another verifier is installed, but AndroidTrustManagerVerifier.EnsureRegistered discards the result and marks itself registered (AndroidTrustManagerVerifier.cs:41-47), so a pre-installed verifier silently replaces the Android trust manager. More seams sit in the handshake path: SslStreamTlsProvider._alpnDisabled/_handshakeOverride (SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:46-72, :161, :192, :310-311), a [Preserve]d test constructor (BouncyCastleTlsProvider.cs:39-45) and a [Preserve]d setter (BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:75-76) kept in players because tests reach the glue by reflection; tests also call the private TurboTlsAuthentication.ValidateLeaf by name (Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/TlsHostnameValidationTests.cs:81).

**Failure scenario.** Auditing 'what does a shipped BouncyCastle build trust' requires proving that s_testTrustAnchors is empty and s_platformVerifier is the expected delegate, both of which are process-wide statics writable by any assembly named TurboHTTP.Soak/Fuzz/H2Interop/TlsInterop/Tests.Runtime (for example a bundled third-party package or a leftover test assembly in a release build). One AddTestTrustAnchor call makes every BouncyCastle connection on iOS/Android skip the OS verifier (network security config, pins, CT) for the rest of the process. Conversely a regression in the iOS/Android native verifier cannot be caught by the loopback suites, because they run through X509Chain.

## Suggested fix
Move the anchor injection below the platform seam (pass anchors to each native verifier as Windows/macOS already do, add them to the iOS bridge and Android KeyStore path) and delete the X509Chain engine from production, or compile it and the Add/Restore/Exchange statics only under a test define. Drop InternalsVisibleTo for harness names from the shipped assembly (link the sources or use a test define). Make EnsureRegistered fail closed when its verifier is not the installed one. Give the BouncyCastle tests their own define-constrained asmdef with InternalsVisibleTo from the glue instead of [Preserve]d reflection seams.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The X509Chain test engine and the Add/Restore anchor statics are compiled only under a test define, or the anchors are passed below the platform seam
- [ ] InternalsVisibleTo entries for harness assembly names are removed from the shipped assembly
- [ ] EnsureRegistered fails closed when its verifier is not the installed one
- [ ] Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ contains a deterministic NUnit test asserting no anchors are honoured without the test define, which fails before the fix

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `tls-design-05` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/tls.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: low. Angle: architecture.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: The facts hold, the security framing does not. Verify branches on the process-wide test-anchor array before the platform verifier (ServerCertificateVerifier.cs:286-291) and the X509Chain engine with AllowUnknownCertificateAuthority is compiled unconditionally (:341-353, :356-450); Add/Restore are plain internals (:303-334); InternalsVisibleTo names five unsigned non-shipped assemblies (Runtime/Transport/AssemblyInfo.cs:3-13); PlatformVerifierTrustsTestAnchors is Windows/macOS only (:228-229); AndroidTrustManagerVerifier.EnsureRegistered discards RegisterPlatformVerifier's result (AndroidTrustManagerVerifier.cs:41-47); test seams and [Preserve]d reflection hooks exist (SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:46-72, BouncyCastleTlsProvider.cs:39-45, BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:75-76). But reaching any of these needs code already running in the app with internals access (an assembly the app developer ships under a harness name), which can do anything anyway; production registers no anchor, and without one the X509Chain path is unreachable (:290) and its result is still rejected unless the root is an anchor (:419-423). On Android s_platformVerifier starts null, so the discarded result only matters after another internal caller registered first. The device-coverage point is real but known and partly mitigated: #239 already records that loopback cases 'use test anchors, which a player serves through X509Chain rather than JNI', and the native Android verifier is exercised by ServerCertificateVerifierTests.PublicChain (clears anchors) and ExternalNetwork rows on devices; iOS device rows remain owed under #239/#99. Architecture/code-smell, low.

title: [TLS] SslStreamTlsProvider has no handshake deadline, so a peer that never answers the ClientHello holds the connection for the whole request timeout
body:
## Summary
WrapAsync waits for AuthenticateAsClientAsync bounded only by the caller's token, which is the request timeout. The connect deadline ends at TCP connect, and the BouncyCastle provider has its own 30 s bound. Behind a captive portal that black-holes TLS, a request with a long or infinite timeout keeps its socket and permits for that whole time. The tunnel handshake has the same gap.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:213`

## Problem
WrapAsync starts the authentication and waits with AbandonableTask.WaitAsync(authTask, ct) (SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:213-214); the only bound is the caller's token. TcpConnectionPool.CreateConnectionAsync passes the request token straight through (TcpConnectionPool.cs:684-685): the connect timeout ended when the socket connected (ConnectWithDeadlineAsync) and DNS has its own bound, but TLS has none. The request token is CancelAfter(request.Timeout) (RawSocketTransport.cs:439-440), which the caller may set to minutes or Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan for downloads (UHttpRequest.WithTimeout). The BouncyCastle provider got an independent 30 s bound for exactly this reason (#142; BouncyCastleTlsProvider.cs:102-111, remarks 68-76), SslStream did not, and the same gap applies to the CONNECT-tunnel handshake (RawSocketTransport.cs:1458-1462).

**Failure scenario.** Mobile client behind a captive portal or middlebox that completes the TCP handshake and black-holes TLS, request made with a 10 minute (or infinite) timeout for a large download: connect succeeds in milliseconds, AuthenticateAsClientAsync never completes, and the request, its socket, its per-host and global permits stay held for 10 minutes (or forever) instead of failing at a handshake bound comparable to the connect timeout.

## Suggested fix
Give SslStreamTlsProvider.WrapAsync the same linked deadline as the BouncyCastle provider (shared constant, IOException with inner TimeoutException), racing the handshake against it through AbandonableTask and disposing the SslStream in the existing catch.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] SslStreamTlsProvider.WrapAsync applies the same linked handshake deadline as the BouncyCastle provider, using a shared constant, and fails with an IOException wrapping a TimeoutException
- [ ] The CONNECT tunnel handshake is bounded the same way
- [ ] The SslStream is disposed on the deadline path
- [ ] Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ contains a deterministic NUnit test with a server that accepts TCP and never answers, using a long request timeout, which fails before the fix

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `tls-runtime-03` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/tls.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: low. Angle: resource-management.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. SslStreamTlsProvider.WrapAsync bounds the handshake only by the caller token (SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:213-214, AbandonableTask.WaitAsync(authTask, ct)); TcpConnectionPool.CreateConnectionAsync passes the request token (TcpConnectionPool.cs:684-685) and the connect deadline covers only the TCP connect (ConnectSocketAsync :750; ConnectionPoolOptions.cs:116-118 documents 'after DNS and before TLS'). The token is CancelAfter(request.Timeout) (RawSocketTransport.cs:439-440). BouncyCastle has its own 30 s bound (BouncyCastleTlsProvider.cs:102-111); the tunnel handshake has the same gap (RawSocketTransport.cs:1458-1462). No handshake-specific bound found for SslStream. Downgraded: the default request timeout is 30-45 s (PlatformConfig.cs:21-26), equal to BouncyCastle's bound, so the gap exists only when the caller raises the request timeout, and then a server that completes TLS and never answers holds the same connection and permits for the same time (there is no response-header deadline on fresh connections either). It is a provider inconsistency and slower failure on TLS black holes, not an unbounded hold beyond what the caller configured.

Also reported as `tls-protocol-12` (merged into this issue).

Related: #344.

title: [TLS] SslStream provider cannot detect TLS truncation, so cut close-delimited HTTP/1.1 bodies are accepted as complete
body:
## Summary
WrapAsync returns the raw SslStream, which reports 0 on a transport close at a record boundary whether or not close_notify arrived. Only the BouncyCastle provider enforces close_notify and has a truncation test. A response with no Content-Length or chunking, cut by an on-path TCP FIN, is returned as a successful shorter body on the default backend.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:232`

## Problem
WrapAsync returns the raw SslStream (lines 232-237). SslStream reports end of stream (0) when the transport closes on a record boundary whether or not close_notify arrived, and .NET Standard 2.1 exposes no way to tell. Only the BouncyCastle provider enforces close_notify (TurboTlsClient.RequiresCloseNotify, TurboTlsClient.cs:102) and only it has a truncation test (Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/BouncyCastleTruncationTests.cs). Http11ResponseBodySource.ReadToEndAsync (Runtime/Transport/Http1/Http11ResponseBodySource.cs:389-399) completes the body on a 0-byte read. No customer document mentions the difference.

**Failure scenario.** TlsBackend.Auto/SslStream, HTTP/1.1 response without Content-Length or chunking (HTTP/1.0 origin, some proxies). An on-path attacker injects a TCP FIN after a chosen record; the client returns the shortened body as a successful response. Confirm per runtime with the BouncyCastleTruncationTests server run against the SslStream provider.

## Spec reference
RFC 9112 section 9.8; RFC 8446 section 6.1

## Suggested fix
Run the truncation test against SslStream on each runtime to record the actual behaviour; if it cannot be detected, mark close-delimited responses received over SslStream as unverifiable (documented, or surfaced on the response) rather than silently complete.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The existing BouncyCastleTruncationTests server is run against the SslStream provider on each supported runtime and the observed behaviour is recorded
- [ ] If truncation is undetectable, close-delimited responses over SslStream are documented as unverifiable or flagged on the response
- [ ] Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ contains an NUnit truncation test for the SslStream provider asserting the recorded behaviour

## Context

title: [TLS] SslStreamTlsProvider silently drops ALPN protocol names other than h2 and http/1.1
body:
## Summary
BuildAlpnOptions adds only the h2 and http/1.1 values and skips any other string, while the BouncyCastle provider sends every name. An offer made only of unknown names produces a handshake without ALPN and NegotiatedAlpn of null, with no error. A test asserts this behaviour. It is not reachable from the built-in HTTP paths.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:352`

## Problem
BuildAlpnOptions adds only SslApplicationProtocol.Http2 and Http11 and skips any other string (SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:348-356, documented at :337-338) although SslApplicationProtocol has a string constructor; the BouncyCastle provider sends every offered name (TurboTlsClient.cs:134-142). ShouldNegotiateAlpn treats a non-empty offer as 'negotiate' (:399-405), so an offer made only of unknown names produces options with an empty protocol list, a handshake without ALPN and NegotiatedAlpn == null, indistinguishable from 'server selected nothing'. The same offer on a runtime without ALPN throws PlatformNotSupportedException (:407-412). ITlsProvider documents alpnProtocols as an arbitrary preference list (ITlsProvider.cs:19-23) and the provider is reachable publicly through TlsProviderSelector.GetProvider. Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/SslStreamAlpnOptionsTests.cs:33 (BuildAlpnOptions_SkipsUnknownProtocols_FreshListPerCall) pins the dropping.

**Failure scenario.** A caller of the public provider (or a future internal protocol such as a gRPC or custom ALPN id) offers ["my-proto"] on a runtime with SslStream ALPN: the handshake succeeds with no ALPN extension and no error, where BouncyCastle would have offered the protocol and the no-ALPN runtime would have thrown. Not reachable from the built-in HTTP paths, which only offer h2/http/1.1.

## Suggested fix
Pass unknown names through with new SslApplicationProtocol(name), or reject them with the same PlatformNotSupportedException rule as the no-ALPN case; update the test to the chosen contract.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] SslStreamTlsProvider passes unknown names through as SslApplicationProtocol(name), or rejects them with the same PlatformNotSupportedException rule used when ALPN is unavailable
- [ ] The existing test is updated to the chosen contract
- [ ] Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ contains a deterministic NUnit test offering only an unknown name that fails before the fix

## Context

title: [TLS] SslStream ALPN options leave AllowRenegotiation enabled when h2 is offered
body:
## Summary
SslStreamTlsProvider.BuildAlpnOptions sets only TargetHost, EnabledSslProtocols and ApplicationProtocols, so SslClientAuthenticationOptions.AllowRenegotiation keeps its default of true. RFC 9113 section 9.2.1 forbids TLS renegotiation on HTTP/2 connections, and the BouncyCastle path already refuses it. It affects runtimes where SslStream negotiates ALPN (CoreCLR), not Unity's Mono/IL2CPP today.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:360`

## Problem
BuildAlpnOptions sets only TargetHost, EnabledSslProtocols and ApplicationProtocols (lines 360-365); SslClientAuthenticationOptions.AllowRenegotiation defaults to true. The same options object is used when 'h2' is in the offer. The BouncyCastle path refuses renegotiation (Lib/tls/TlsClientProtocol.cs:751-765).

**Failure scenario.** On a runtime whose SslStream negotiates ALPN (IsAlpnSupported() true; not Unity's Mono/IL2CPP today, where the probe returns false), an HTTP/2 connection over TLS 1.2 accepts a server-initiated renegotiation after the connection preface instead of treating it as a connection error. Confirm on a CoreCLR runtime against a TLS 1.2 server that sends HelloRequest.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 section 9.2.1

## Suggested fix
Set AllowRenegotiation = false in BuildAlpnOptions whenever 'h2' is offered.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] BuildAlpnOptions sets AllowRenegotiation = false whenever h2 is in the ALPN offer
- [ ] A server-initiated renegotiation on an h2 connection over TLS 1.2 fails the connection instead of being accepted
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ asserts the options object produced for an h2 offer has AllowRenegotiation false and fails before the fix
