title: [TLS] BouncyCastle host-name check falls back to the subject CN, accepting certificates the Android platform verifier rejects
body:
## Summary
TlsCertificateNameMatcher accepts a single subject CN when the leaf has no subjectAltName. On Android the native verifier does not match the host name, so this matcher is the only host check, and a CN-only certificate issued under a trusted or name-constrained CA is accepted although HttpsURLConnection and OkHttp reject it. RFC 9525 removed CN-ID matching. Android players using TlsBackend.BouncyCastle are affected.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/TlsCertificateNameMatcher.cs:64`

## Problem
TlsCertificateNameMatcher.Matches returns `commonNames.Count == 1 && MatchesDnsPattern(commonNames[0], target)` when the certificate has no subjectAltName (lines 64-69). TurboTlsAuthentication.ValidateHostname (Runtime/Transport/BouncyCastle/TurboTlsAuthentication.cs:106-149) is the BouncyCastle host check. On Windows and Apple the platform SSL policy also receives the host (WindowsCertificateVerifier.cs:162-181, MacSecTrustVerifier.cs:103, TurboHttpSecTrustVerifier.mm:181) and can still reject, but on Android the verifier explicitly does not match the host: AndroidTrustManagerVerifier.cs:23-25 ('it does not match the host name (Android leaves that to HostnameVerifier), so TlsCertificateNameMatcher stays the host check'). Android's default HostnameVerifier stopped using the CN in Android 9, and RFC 9525 removed CN-ID. Tests assert the fallback: Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/BouncyCastleChainValidationTests.cs:79-81 (LeafCnOnly accepted) and TlsCertificateNameMatcherTests.cs:86. The decision predates the native verifiers (Development~/docs/implementation-journal/2026-11-bc-chain-validation.md:56).

**Failure scenario.** Android player with TlsBackend.BouncyCastle. A CA the device trusts (a dNSName name-constrained sub-CA, or a private/enterprise CA) issues a certificate with CN=api.victim.com and no subjectAltName. dNSName name constraints do not apply to a CN, so the Android trust manager returns a path; the managed matcher then matches the CN and the handshake succeeds. HttpsURLConnection/OkHttp on the same device reject that certificate. This is 'a certificate the platform would reject' (CLAUDE.md section 3).

## Spec reference
RFC 9525 section 6 (CN-ID removed); RFC 6125 6.4.4 (CN only a MAY)

## Suggested fix
Drop the CN fallback from TlsCertificateNameMatcher (SAN only, RFC 9525), or at least disable it where no platform host policy runs (Android). Update the two tests that assert CN acceptance.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] TlsCertificateNameMatcher matches the host against subjectAltName only (RFC 9525 section 6); a leaf without a SAN never matches
- [ ] A BouncyCastle handshake to a host presenting a CN-only certificate fails with a CertificateError
- [ ] The two tests that assert CN acceptance (BouncyCastleChainValidationTests LeafCnOnly, TlsCertificateNameMatcherTests) are updated to assert rejection
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ fails before the fix

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `tls-protocol-01` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/tls.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: security.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. TlsCertificateNameMatcher.cs:64-69 accepts a single subject CN when the leaf has no subjectAltName; TurboTlsAuthentication.ValidateHostname (TurboTlsAuthentication.cs:106-149) is the only host check the BouncyCastle path owns. On Android the registered verifier calls X509TrustManagerExtensions.checkServerTrusted(chain, "RSA", host) (AndroidTrustManagerVerifier.cs:118-122), which uses the host for per-domain config/pins only; the file says so itself (lines 23-25: 'it does not match the host name ... TlsCertificateNameMatcher stays the host check'). So a CN-only leaf under any anchor the Android trust manager accepts passes; Android's own HostnameVerifier ignores the CN since Android 9. Apple is guarded (SecPolicyCreateSSL with host: TurboHttpSecTrustVerifier.mm:181, MacSecTrustVerifier.cs:103, which rejects CN-only), Windows crypt32's SSL policy (WindowsCertificateVerifier.cs:162-181) also honours the CN, so the divergence from the platform is Android-only. Tests pin the behaviour (BouncyCastleChainValidationTests.cs:79-81). No guard found. Mitigating: deliberate and documented (journal 2026-11-bc-chain-validation.md:56, RFC 6125 6.4.4 MAY, which CLAUDE.md names as oracle), and exploitation needs a trusted CA to issue a SAN-less certificate (forbidden for public CAs), so it is a hardening/policy gap against CLAUDE.md section 3 rather than a directly exploitable hole. Whether Android's path validator applies dNSName constraints to the CN (the sub-CA scenario) is not settled statically. Not tracked by an open issue.

Related: #33, #239.

title: [TLS] TlsPlatformCapabilities caches its summary forever, so SystemKnownBroken and Recommended ignore failures recorded later
body:
## Summary
TlsPlatformCapabilities.GetSummary returns a cached value sampled once from TlsProviderSelector.IsSslStreamKnownBroken. MarkSslStreamBroken and MarkSslStreamViable change that state without invalidating the cache, so only provider registration refreshes it. Support logs and the HTTP monitor therefore report SystemKnownBroken=False after a platform TLS failure.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/TlsPlatformCapabilities.cs:65`

## Problem
GetSummary returns s_cached.Value (TlsPlatformCapabilities.cs:60-65); Evaluate samples TlsProviderSelector.IsSslStreamKnownBroken() once (line 102). MarkSslStreamBroken and MarkSslStreamViable change that state (TlsProviderSelector.cs:138-158) without calling TlsPlatformCapabilities.Invalidate(); only provider registration invalidates (TlsProviderSelector.cs:110-111).

**Failure scenario.** An app logs GetDiagnosticSummary() at startup (the documented use), then the first Auto handshake hits a platform TLS failure and MarkSslStreamBroken runs: later summaries (support logs, the HTTP monitor) still report SystemKnownBroken=False and Recommended=SslStream.

## Suggested fix
Call TlsPlatformCapabilities.Invalidate() on the 0/1 -> 2 and 0 -> 1 transitions in TlsProviderSelector.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] After MarkSslStreamBroken or MarkSslStreamViable, the next GetSummary reflects the new state without a test-only refresh
- [ ] TlsProviderSelector calls TlsPlatformCapabilities.Invalidate() on the 0 to 1 and 0 to 2 viability transitions
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ takes a summary, marks SslStream broken, and asserts the next summary changes; it fails before the fix

## Context

title: [TLS] Public TlsPlatformCapabilities summary reports a constant, a stale flag and a recommendation that carries no information
body:
## Summary
IsSystemTlsAvailable is true on every supported runtime, SystemProviderDescription is always SslStream, IsSystemTlsKnownBroken is cached and goes stale, and RecommendedBackend returns SslStream or Auto, which resolve to the same provider and never BouncyCastle. Its stated rationale that BouncyCastle lacks chain validation no longer holds. The public struct also exposes five undocumented fields, so apps logging the summary get misleading data.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/TlsPlatformCapabilities.cs:95`

## Problem
IsSystemTlsAvailable is computed from TlsProviderSelector.GetProvider(TlsBackend.SslStream) != null (TlsPlatformCapabilities.cs:117-132), which returns the static SslStreamTlsProvider.Instance (TlsProviderSelector.cs:70-73) and whose type initializer is written never to throw (SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:94-125): the field is true on every supported runtime and SystemProviderDescription is always "SslStream". The two catch blocks at :134-145 are identical. IsSystemTlsKnownBroken is read once into a Lazy (:60, :90-93) and the cache is invalidated only by BouncyCastle registration (TlsProviderSelector.cs:110-111, :121); MarkSslStreamBroken (:151-158) does not invalidate it, so a summary taken at startup (the documented use: 'startup logs') keeps reporting false after platform TLS failures. The test that covers the flag hides this by calling the internal RefreshForTesting first (Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/TlsPlatformCapabilitiesTests.cs:99-109). RecommendedBackend is SslStream or Auto (:160-171), which resolve to the same provider instance, and never BouncyCastle; its justification ('Never recommend a provider without full certificate chain validation (BouncyCastle today)', :167-169 and :19-20) is no longer true (BouncyCastle validates through the OS verifiers). The public struct exposes five undocumented public fields (:12-16).

**Failure scenario.** An app logs TlsPlatformCapabilities.GetDiagnosticSummary() at startup and again after HTTPS starts failing with a platform TLS exception: both lines say SystemKnownBroken=False, Recommended=SslStream. On Unity with BouncyCastle registered (the only way to get HTTP/2) the summary still recommends SslStream, and when SslStream is known broken it recommends Auto, which is the same broken provider.

## Suggested fix
Either delete the type or make it truthful: compute the summary on demand (it is not on a hot path), drop IsSystemTlsAvailable/RecommendedBackend or define them in terms of ALPN and verifier availability, document the fields, and remove the duplicate catch.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] TlsPlatformCapabilities is either removed or computed on demand with fields that can differ between platforms (ALPN support, verifier availability)
- [ ] RecommendedBackend and IsSystemTlsAvailable are removed or defined in terms of ALPN and verifier availability, and every public field has XML docs
- [ ] The duplicate catch blocks are removed

title: [TLS] TlsProviderSelector invokes the user-supplied DiagnosticLogger unguarded on the connection path
body:
## Summary
TlsProviderSelector.Log calls DiagnosticLogger without try/catch. MarkSslStreamViable runs it inside TcpConnectionPool's handshake try block, so a throwing logger tears down a connection whose handshake succeeded and fails the request as Unknown. MarkSslStreamBroken runs it in the catch block before stream.Dispose(), so a throwing logger skips the dispose and replaces the TLS error. The logger runs on connection threads, where Unity APIs other than Debug.Log throw.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/TlsProviderSelector.cs:49`

## Problem
Log is DiagnosticLogger?.Invoke(message) with no try/catch (TlsProviderSelector.cs:49). MarkSslStreamViable calls it after the first successful handshake (:140-141), from inside TcpConnectionPool's try block and before the secure stream is adopted (TcpConnectionPool.cs:686-691): an exception from the delegate lands in the catch at :696, which disposes the raw stream and rethrows, so the connection that just handshook is torn down and the request fails with UHttpErrorType.Unknown. MarkSslStreamBroken calls Log from inside that catch block before stream.Dispose() (:700-703): if the delegate throws there, the dispose is skipped (socket left to the finalizer) and the logger's exception replaces the TLS failure. The delegate runs on connection threads; the documented example uses Debug.Log, but any Unity API other than Debug.Log throws UnityException off the main thread. The static also persists across play sessions without domain reload (no reset hook).

**Failure scenario.** TlsProviderSelector.DiagnosticLogger = msg => statusLabel.text = msg; the first HTTPS request of the session fails with an Unknown error wrapping UnityException although the TLS handshake succeeded; the state is already 'viable', so later requests work and the failure is not reproducible.

## Suggested fix
Wrap the invocation in try/catch (diagnostics must never change control flow), and call Mark* outside the handshake try/after the dispose.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Log catches and swallows exceptions from DiagnosticLogger
- [ ] A throwing DiagnosticLogger does not fail a successful handshake and does not mask the original TLS failure
- [ ] The raw stream is disposed on every failure path even when the logger throws
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ with a throwing logger fails before the fix

title: [TLS] ITlsProvider is public but cannot be plugged in for HTTP; the selector is a closed enum with a hard-coded BouncyCastle slot
body:
## Summary
ITlsProvider, TlsResult and TlsProviderSelector are public, but selection is a three-value TlsBackend switch with one internal BouncyCastle registration slot and no HTTP-side provider option. The only public entry is WebSocketConnectionOptions.TlsProvider, typed object and cast at run time. Provider identity is checked with ProviderName == "SslStream" strings, WrapAsync has no options parameter, and innerStream disposal on failure is undocumented. A customer or the planned native backend cannot use a custom provider for UHttpClient.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/TlsProviderSelector.cs:54`

## Problem
ITlsProvider, TlsResult and TlsProviderSelector are public (ITlsProvider.cs:12, TlsResult.cs:9, TlsProviderSelector.cs:11), but selection is GetProvider(TlsBackend) over a three-value Core enum (TlsProviderSelector.cs:54-68; an unknown value silently maps to Auto in the default arm). The only registration hook is internal and provider-specific: one static field _bouncyCastleProvider (:19), RegisterBouncyCastleProvider (:105-112, internal, reachable only through InternalsVisibleTo), IsBouncyCastleAvailable (:80). HTTP has no provider option at all: TcpConnectionPool's resolver is a test seam on an internal constructor (TcpConnectionPool.cs:282-283, :385). The single place a third-party ITlsProvider is accepted is WebSocketConnectionOptions.TlsProvider, typed object and cast at run time (Runtime/WebSocket/WebSocketConnectionOptions.cs:107-111, RawSocketWebSocketTransport.cs:286-296). Concrete providers leak through the abstraction: callers identify the provider by tlsResult.ProviderName == "SslStream" (TcpConnectionPool.cs:688, RawSocketTransport.cs:1520) and the HTTP/2 capability probe names both providers (RawSocketTransport.cs:129-139). The interface itself has no options parameter (client certificates, pinning #117, minimum version) and does not state who disposes innerStream on failure: SslStream can throw before it owns the stream (SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:169-196: argument checks, ShouldNegotiateAlpn :410, ResolveAlpnOptions :294) and BouncyCastle documents 'on any failure the inner stream is disposed' (BouncyCastleTlsProvider.cs:60-62) yet throws at :98 without disposing; all three callers compensate with their own Dispose.

**Failure scenario.** The planned native TLS backend (#429) or a customer provider needs a new TlsBackend enum value in Core, another Register*/Is*Available pair in the selector, another term in ProbeCapabilities and another string in the viability checks; a customer can implement the public ITlsProvider today but can use it only for WebSocket, not for UHttpClient. Any future parameter added to WrapAsync is a breaking change for those WebSocket implementers. A custom provider that returns ProviderName "SslStream" is counted as the platform provider by the diagnostics state.

## Suggested fix
Either make the abstraction real (a registry keyed by backend with one internal Register(TlsBackend, ITlsProvider), an options object on WrapAsync, a documented innerStream ownership rule, provider identity by reference) or make ITlsProvider/TlsResult internal and type the WebSocket option accordingly. Remove the string comparisons in favour of a property on the provider.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Either the abstraction is made real (internal Register(TlsBackend, ITlsProvider), an options object on WrapAsync, documented innerStream ownership, provider identity by property) or ITlsProvider and TlsResult become internal and the WebSocket option is typed accordingly
- [ ] String comparisons of ProviderName are replaced by a provider property
- [ ] The innerStream disposal rule on failure is documented and implemented consistently in both providers and all callers
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ covers the chosen contract

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `tls-design-03` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/tls.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: architecture.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: The facts hold. ITlsProvider, TlsResult and TlsProviderSelector are public (ITlsProvider.cs:12, TlsResult.cs:9, TlsProviderSelector.cs:11); selection is a closed switch whose default arm maps unknown values to Auto (TlsProviderSelector.cs:54-68) with one hard-coded internal slot (:19, :105-112). HTTP has no provider option (the resolver is an internal test constructor, TcpConnectionPool.cs:282-283, :384-386); the only public entry for a custom provider is WebSocketConnectionOptions.TlsProvider typed object (WebSocketConnectionOptions.cs:107-111) cast at run time (RawSocketWebSocketTransport ResolveTlsProvider). Provider identity is a string compare (TcpConnectionPool.cs:688, RawSocketTransport.cs:1520). Ownership of innerStream on failure is not in the interface docs (ITlsProvider.cs:13-37); BouncyCastle documents 'on any failure the inner stream is disposed' (BouncyCastleTlsProvider.cs:60-62) yet throws at :93-98 without disposing, and SslStream can throw before it owns the stream (SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:169-196, :409); the pool compensates (TcpConnectionPool.cs:703). No wrong behaviour today: this is a public-API/pluggability finding (a public interface that cannot gain a parameter without breaking implementers, relevant to #429 and #117), not a runtime defect.

Related: #117, #429, [[R11-tls-design-08]], [[R11-tls-design-15]].

title: [TLS] An unusable BouncyCastle selection is discovered only after connecting, and IsBouncyCastleAvailable and SupportsHttp2 report true on Linux
body:
## Summary
The TLS provider is resolved after DNS, TCP connect and any proxy CONNECT, so TlsBackend.BouncyCastle without the define opens and closes a connection per request and fails as UHttpErrorType.Unknown, with a message that points at a type that does not exist. On Linux BouncyCastle registers and reports available, although the verifier rejects every chain, so PlatformConfig.SupportsHttp2 is true and each https request fails with a certificate error after a full connect.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/TlsProviderSelector.cs:85`

## Problem
The provider is resolved inside the per-connection handshake block, after DNS and TCP connect (TcpConnectionPool.cs:659-683), and for proxied requests after the CONNECT exchange (RawSocketTransport.cs:1453-1455). With TlsBackend.BouncyCastle and no define, GetBouncyCastleProvider throws InvalidOperationException (TlsProviderSelector.cs:85-98) each time, mapped to UHttpErrorType.Unknown (RawSocketTransport.cs:826-827) rather than InvalidRequest; neither RawSocketTransport nor TcpConnectionPool validates the backend at construction or before connecting. The message advises calling BouncyCastleModuleRegistration.EnsureRegistered() (:93-94), which cannot help when the define is missing (the type does not exist) and is not callable from Assembly-CSharp because the glue asmdef is autoReferenced: false. On Linux the provider registers and IsBouncyCastleAvailable() returns true (:80-83) although ServerCertificateVerifier rejects every chain there (ServerCertificateVerifier.cs:293-294, :239-241): each request completes TCP and most of a TLS handshake before failing as CertificateError, and RawSocketTransport.ProbeCapabilities reports TransportCapabilities.Http2 from that flag (RawSocketTransport.cs:129-139), so PlatformConfig.SupportsHttp2 is true. The define is set per build-target group and Standalone covers Windows, macOS and Linux together.

**Failure scenario.** A project enables TURBOHTTP_BOUNCYCASTLE for Standalone to get HTTP/2 on Windows and macOS; its Linux build (or Linux Editor) reports SupportsHttp2 = true and IsBouncyCastleAvailable = true, then fails every https request after a full connect with a certificate error. A project that sets TlsBackend.BouncyCastle but forgot the define opens and closes a TCP connection (or a proxy tunnel) to the origin for every request and gets error type Unknown.

## Suggested fix
Resolve and validate the provider before any socket work (at transport construction lazily on first use, or first thing in GetConnectionAsync) and report a configuration error (InvalidRequest). Let the selector refuse BouncyCastle, and report it unavailable, on a platform with no certificate verifier, and correct the error message's advice.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The provider is resolved and validated before any socket work, and a missing or unsupported BouncyCastle backend raises UHttpException with UHttpErrorType.InvalidRequest and an accurate message
- [ ] IsBouncyCastleAvailable and the HTTP/2 capability probe report false on platforms where the verifier rejects all chains (Linux)
- [ ] No TCP connection is opened for a request whose TLS backend is unusable
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ fails before the fix

title: [TLS] SslStream viability state is maintained by callers instead of the provider, and the three call sites diverge
body:
## Summary
TlsProviderSelector keeps a process-wide viability state that callers update. TcpConnectionPool marks both outcomes, the CONNECT tunnel path marks success only, RawSocketWebSocketTransport marks neither, and all update only under TlsBackend.Auto. The Broken state is sticky, is never cleared in production and survives Enter Play Mode without domain reload, so one transient NotSupportedException can mark SslStream broken for the rest of the process.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/TlsProviderSelector.cs:138`

## Problem
TlsProviderSelector holds a process-wide _sslStreamViabilityState (TlsProviderSelector.cs:23-26) that callers must update through MarkSslStreamViable/MarkSslStreamBroken (:138-158). TcpConnectionPool marks both outcomes (TcpConnectionPool.cs:688-689, :700-701); the CONNECT tunnel handshake marks success only and has no failure path (RawSocketTransport.cs:1455-1464, :1518-1522); RawSocketWebSocketTransport marks neither (no reference to either method). All sites update only when the backend is Auto, so a client configured with TlsBackend.SslStream is never recorded, and they detect the provider by string (ProviderName == "SslStream"). The state is sticky: Broken is never cleared in production (ResetProbeState is test-only, :163-164) and survives Enter Play Mode without domain reload because the engine-free assembly has no reset hook and TurboHttpBootstrap does not reset it.

**Failure scenario.** A platform TLS failure during a proxied or WebSocket handshake is never recorded, while one transient NotSupportedException on a direct connection (the documented false positive at :179-182) marks SslStream 'known broken' for the rest of the process and for every later play session in the Editor.

## Suggested fix
Record the outcome inside SslStreamTlsProvider.WrapAsync, the one place that knows it, or remove the state together with the summary flag it feeds (see tls-design-07).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Viability is recorded inside SslStreamTlsProvider.WrapAsync (or the state is removed together with the summary flag), so every call path records it consistently
- [ ] A transient failure does not permanently mark SslStream broken, and the state is reset on Editor domain-reload-free play sessions
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ covers a proxied and a WebSocket handshake failure and fails before the fix

title: [TLS] TlsResult.CipherSuite is documented as a suite name but holds a hex code or null, is read by nothing, and dead parameters remain
body:
## Summary
The public TlsResult.CipherSuite documents IANA names such as TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, while BouncyCastle fills a hex string (0x1301) and SslStream passes null. No runtime code reads the property, yet each BouncyCastle handshake allocates the string. The three-argument TurboTlsClient constructor, the CancellationToken parameter of BouncyCastleTlsStream.HandshakeAsync and the handshake timeout plumbing are also unused.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/TlsResult.cs:43`

## Problem
The public TlsResult.CipherSuite doc gives 'TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256' as the example (TlsResult.cs:35-43). BouncyCastle supplies FormatCipherSuite's "0x{cipherSuite:X4}" (TurboTlsClient.cs:171, :189-192), SslStream always passes null (SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:236), and no code in Runtime reads the property (the pool copies only NegotiatedAlpn, TlsVersion and ProviderName, TcpConnectionPool.cs:691-694; RawSocketTransport.cs:1395-1404). Other unused pieces in the same path: the three-argument TurboTlsClient constructor (TurboTlsClient.cs:65-68, production uses the four-argument one at BouncyCastleTlsProvider.cs:180), the CancellationToken parameter of BouncyCastleTlsStream.HandshakeAsync that production always passes as None (BouncyCastleTlsProvider.cs:188), and the handshake timeout plumbed into TurboTlsClient.GetHandshakeTimeoutMillis that the engine never reads in non-blocking mode (TurboTlsClient.cs:92-96).

**Failure scenario.** A consumer of the public TlsResult (through TlsProviderSelector.GetProvider().WrapAsync or a WebSocket provider wrapper) logs or compares CipherSuite against IANA names per the doc and gets "0x1301" or null; each BouncyCastle handshake allocates a string nobody reads.

## Suggested fix
Either surface the value (IANA name, and carry it to the connection diagnostics) or remove the property before 1.0; delete the unused constructor and the dead token parameter.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] TlsResult.CipherSuite is either filled with an IANA name by both providers and carried to connection diagnostics, or removed before 1.0
- [ ] The unused TurboTlsClient constructor, the dead CancellationToken parameter and unread timeout plumbing are removed
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ asserts the documented contract of the retained property or compiles against its removal

title: [Packaging] BouncyCastle-only certificate verifier stack compiles into the always-included Transport assembly and into every platform
body:
## Summary
ServerCertificateVerifier, PlatformVerifierRunner and the Windows, macOS and Apple verifiers (about 1,700 lines and 35 DllImports) are referenced only by the opt-in BouncyCastle glue but live in TurboHTTP.Transport. The Windows and macOS P/Invoke files have no platform guard, so they ship in Android and iOS assemblies, and the iOS SecTrust bridge has no define constraint and compiles into every Xcode project. The cost is tens of KB of dead weight in builds that do not strip.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/WindowsCertificateVerifier.cs:24`

## Problem
ServerCertificateVerifier, PlatformVerifierRunner, WindowsCertificateVerifier, MacSecTrustVerifier and AppleTrustVerifier (477 + 249 + 445 + 346 + 182 = 1,699 lines, about 35 DllImports) are referenced only by the opt-in glue (TurboTlsAuthentication.cs:76-78, :204) yet sit in TurboHTTP.Transport, which every project compiles. The Windows and macOS files have no platform guard by design ('Compiled on every platform (the import resolves on first call), installed only on Windows', WindowsCertificateVerifier.cs:21-22; MacSecTrustVerifier.cs:23-24), so crypt32 and Security.framework P/Invoke declarations are part of Android and iOS assemblies; the platform choice is an #if ladder written twice (ServerCertificateVerifier.cs:144-155 and :211-221). The iOS bridge Plugins/iOS/TurboHttpSecTrustVerifier.mm has defineConstraints: [] in its .meta, so it is compiled into every iOS Xcode project whether or not TURBOHTTP_BOUNCYCASTLE is set. The Android verifier is the exception and lives in the glue because it needs UnityEngine JNI (AndroidTrustManagerVerifier.cs:14-16), so the 'platform verifier' concept is split across two assemblies with a static registration seam between them.

**Failure scenario.** A project without BouncyCastle built without managed stripping of user assemblies (Mono Disabled, or any level that keeps unreferenced types of non-root assemblies) ships the whole verifier stack and its P/Invoke stubs for other operating systems; an iOS build always compiles the SecTrust bridge. The size is small (tens of KB) but it is dead weight tied to an optional feature, and the Windows/macOS marshalling code is carried on mobile.

## Suggested fix
Guard the P/Invoke halves of the Windows and macOS verifiers with the same #if as DefaultPlatformVerifier (keep the pure mapping functions unconditional for the shadow-build tests), derive CompiledPlatform and DefaultPlatformVerifier from one ladder, and give the iOS plugin the TURBOHTTP_BOUNCYCASTLE define constraint together with an #if on AppleTrustVerifier.Verify (check_repo.py native already models define constraints).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The P/Invoke halves of the Windows and macOS verifiers are guarded by the same #if as DefaultPlatformVerifier, with pure mapping functions kept unconditional
- [ ] CompiledPlatform and DefaultPlatformVerifier derive from one platform ladder
- [ ] The iOS plugin carries the TURBOHTTP_BOUNCYCASTLE define constraint and AppleTrustVerifier.Verify is guarded accordingly; check_repo.py native passes
- [ ] Shadow build and existing verifier tests under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ still pass

title: [TLS] Windows crypt32 verifier disables AuthRoot auto-update, so BouncyCastle rejects chains that SChannel accepts
body:
## Summary
WindowsCertificateVerifier passes CERT_CHAIN_DISABLE_AUTH_ROOT_AUTO_UPDATE to CertGetCertificateChain, so a root the machine has not yet installed from the AuthRoot list is untrusted, while SChannel would fetch it. The stated reason, that evaluation blocks the handshake thread, no longer holds because PlatformVerifierRunner bounds the call at 10 s. The result is a non-retryable CertificateError on a fresh Windows install that works with TlsBackend.SslStream and in a browser.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tls/WindowsCertificateVerifier.cs:39`

## Problem
ChainFlags = CERT_CHAIN_CACHE_ONLY_URL_RETRIEVAL | CERT_CHAIN_DISABLE_AUTH_ROOT_AUTO_UPDATE | CERT_CHAIN_DISABLE_AIA (WindowsCertificateVerifier.cs:39-40), passed to CertGetCertificateChain (line 148). Windows keeps only part of the Microsoft root programme in the ROOT store; the others are listed in the AuthRoot CTL and installed on first use, which this flag forbids. The class remarks admit it (lines 16-17: 'A root the machine has not cached yet is therefore untrusted here even where SChannel would fetch it'). The stated reason (ServerCertificateVerifier.cs:104-106: evaluation runs synchronously on the handshake thread and the deadline cannot interrupt it) no longer holds as written: the call now runs on its own thread bounded at 10 s by PlatformVerifierRunner (PlatformCertificateVerifier.cs:131) and WrapAsync abandons the handshake at the deadline regardless (BouncyCastleTlsProvider.cs:122). The untrusted result maps to unknown_ca -> AuthenticationException -> non-retryable CertificateError (TurboTlsAuthentication.cs:218-220).

**Failure scenario.** Windows Editor or Windows player on a fresh install/VM (or a machine whose browsers use their own root store), TlsBackend.BouncyCastle selected for HTTP/2, server chain ends at a programme root no CryptoAPI client on that machine has used yet: every request fails with a certificate error 'crypt32 chain status 0x00010020/0x00000020', while the same URL works with TlsBackend.SslStream and in a browser. Needs confirmation on a clean Windows image with a host whose root is not preinstalled.

## Suggested fix
Allow the AuthRoot auto-update (drop CERT_CHAIN_DISABLE_AUTH_ROOT_AUTO_UPDATE, keep AIA and revocation off) now that the call is bounded by the runner's timeout, or document the limitation in PlatformNotes and surface a distinct error detail so it is not read as a server fault.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Either CERT_CHAIN_DISABLE_AUTH_ROOT_AUTO_UPDATE is dropped (AIA and revocation stay off) within the runner's timeout, or the limitation is documented in PlatformNotes and surfaced as a distinct error detail
- [ ] Confirmed on a clean Windows image with a host whose root is not preinstalled, and the run recorded
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Tls/ covers the chosen flag set or error detail and fails before the change

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `tls-runtime-04` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/tls.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: platform-compat.

Verification: Plausible: the code is as described; the outcome depends on runtime, device or peer behaviour that a static review cannot settle.

Verifier note: Code is as described: ChainFlags = CERT_CHAIN_CACHE_ONLY_URL_RETRIEVAL | CERT_CHAIN_DISABLE_AUTH_ROOT_AUTO_UPDATE | CERT_CHAIN_DISABLE_AIA (WindowsCertificateVerifier.cs:39-40) passed to CertGetCertificateChain (:148); an untrusted/partial result maps to UntrustedRoot (:218-219) -> unknown_ca -> AuthenticationException (TurboTlsAuthentication.cs:218-220), a non-retryable CertificateError. The limitation is deliberate and stated in the class remarks (:16-17) and, in general terms, in customer docs (Documentation~/Modules/Transport.md:26 'The verifiers never fetch from the network (no revocation check, no intermediate or root download)'), but the Windows consequence (roots that Windows installs lazily from the AuthRoot CTL are untrusted until some other CryptoAPI client has used them) is not spelled out, and the stated reason in ServerCertificateVerifier.cs:104-106 (the deadline cannot interrupt the evaluation) is weaker now that the call runs on a bounded worker (PlatformCertificateVerifier.cs:131). Note that lifting the flag means a Windows Update fetch during verification, which contradicts the verifier contract (PlatformCertificateVerifier.cs:23), so the fix is a trade-off, not a one-line change. Whether real machines hit it (clean installs, Chromium-only users, a Let's Encrypt or similar root not yet installed) cannot be settled statically; no test or record covers a clean Windows image. Not tracked by an open issue.

Also reported as `tls-protocol-07` (merged into this issue).

Related: #258, #286.
